title: How a star's mass decides its ending
text:
Almost everything a star will ever do is settled at birth, and the deciding factor is mass. A star spends most of its existence on what astronomers call the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. The outward pressure generated by that fusion balances the inward pull of gravity, and the star holds its shape for as long as the fuel lasts. Here is the counterintuitive part. The more massive the star, the shorter its life. A heavy star has far more fuel, but it consumes that fuel at an enormously faster rate, so the most massive stars last only a few million years, while a modest star like our Sun lasts billions.

When the core hydrogen runs out, the balance breaks. A Sun-like star swells into a red giant, fuses heavier elements for a time, then sheds its outer layers and leaves behind a white dwarf, a dense ember that slowly cools. A much heavier star collapses catastrophically and explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or a black hole. That explosion scatters the heavy elements forged inside it, which is where the carbon and iron in your own body originally came from.
points: A star's mass is fixed at birth and determines its whole life story.
On the main sequence, hydrogen fuses into helium and that outward pressure balances gravity.
More massive stars live shorter lives because they burn their fuel far faster.
A Sun-like star becomes a red giant and ends as a white dwarf.
A much more massive star explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole.
Supernovae scatter heavy elements, which became the material of planets and of us.
